rewritten_text:
Do you mean—Mr. Knightley?”

“Of course I do. I could never have thought of anyone else, and I supposed you understood that. It seemed perfectly plain when we spoke of him.”

“Not entirely,” replied Emma, struggling for composure, “since everything you said then seemed to refer to another gentleman. I could almost swear you mentioned Mr. Frank Churchill by name. I am certain we discussed the assistance Mr. Frank Churchill gave you when he defended you from the gipsies.”

“Oh, Miss Woodhouse, how strangely you forget!”

“My dear Harriet, I remember exactly the meaning of my own remarks. I said your attachment did not surprise me; that, in view of his service to you, it was most natural. You agreed, speaking with great warmth of your gratitude, and even describing what you had felt on seeing him step forward to save you. My recollection of it is exceedingly clear.”

“Oh dear!” Harriet exclaimed. “Now I understand what you are remembering; but my thoughts were on something quite different. I did not mean the gipsies, nor Mr. Frank Churchill. No!”—with a little animation—“I had in mind a far more precious occasion: Mr. Knightley’s coming to invite me to dance when Mr. Elton refused to dance with me, and when there was nobody else available as a partner. That was the kindness, that was the noble generosity and goodness, that was the service which first taught me how far he stood above every other creature in the world.”

“Good heavens!” cried Emma. “What an unhappy, what a lamentable misunderstanding this has been! What can be done?”

“Then you would not have encouraged me if you had known what I meant? Still, at least I cannot be in a worse position than if the other gentleman had been concerned; and now—it is possible—”

For a few moments she stopped. Emma had no power to speak.

“I am not surprised, Miss Woodhouse,” Harriet continued, “that you see an immense difference between the two, whether in relation to me or to anyone. You must consider one five hundred million times farther above me than the other. But I hope, Miss Woodhouse, supposing—that if—however extraordinary it may seem—. After all, you yourself said that stranger things had happened, that marriages with a greater inequality had occurred than one between Mr. Frank Churchill and me. So it appears that even such a thing as this may have happened before; and if I should have the inexpressible good fortune to—if Mr. Knightley should actually—if he finds no objection in the difference between us, I hope, dear Miss Woodhouse, you will not oppose it or endeavour to place obstacles in our way.

She left everything behind except the memory that these things had happened.

Anne had not returned to Kellynch since leaving Lady Russell’s house in September. There had been no need, and she had managed to avoid the few opportunities that arose to visit the Hall. Now her first return brought her back to the Lodge’s elegant, modern rooms, to the delight of their owner.

Lady Russell’s happiness at seeing her was mixed with some uneasiness. She knew who had been visiting Uppercross. Fortunately, however, Anne had either grown a little fuller and better-looking, or Lady Russell imagined she had. As Anne received her compliments, she was amused to connect them with her cousin’s unspoken admiration, and allowed herself to hope that youth and beauty might blossom for her a second time.

As they talked, she soon became aware of a shift in her own thoughts. The concerns that had filled her heart when she left Kellynch—the ones she had felt the Musgroves disregarded, and that she had been obliged to suppress among them—now interested her less. Lately she had almost forgotten even her father, her sister, and Bath. Their affairs had been submerged by those at Uppercross. Lady Russell returned to the hopes and anxieties they had once shared, expressing satisfaction with the house rented in Camden Place and regret that Mrs. Clay was still staying with them. Anne would have been embarrassed to admit how much more she was thinking about Lyme, Louisa Musgrove, and everyone she knew there. The home and friendship of the Harvilles and Captain Benwick mattered far more to her than her father’s house in Camden Place or her sister’s closeness with Mrs. Clay. She had to make a real effort to appear nearly as concerned as Lady Russell about matters which, naturally, ought to have commanded her first attention.

Another subject initially made their conversation a little awkward. They had to discuss the accident at Lyme. Within five minutes of her arrival the previous day, Lady Russell had been overwhelmed with a full account of everything that had happened. Even so, they must talk about it: she must ask questions, deplore the recklessness, and grieve over its consequences, and both of them must say Captain Wentworth’s name. Anne knew she did this less easily than Lady Russell. She could not speak his name while looking Lady Russell directly in the eye until she found a way around her difficulty by briefly explaining what she believed about the attachment between him and Louisa.

“My nerves can’t stand that sort of thing.”

“But would you really feel comfortable spending the entire evening away from the poor boy?”

“Yes. His father can do it, as you see, so why shouldn’t I? Jemima is so careful, and she could send a message every hour to tell us how he was. I honestly think Charles might as well have told his father that all of us would come. I’m no more worried about little Charles now than he is. Yesterday I was terribly frightened, but things are quite different today.”

“Well, if you think there is still time to let them know, why don’t you go with your husband? Leave little Charles with me. Mr. and Mrs. Musgrove can hardly object while I’m here to look after him.”

“Do you mean it?” cried Mary, her eyes lighting up. “Goodness, what an excellent idea! Truly excellent. Of course, I might as well go, because I’m no use here at home, am I? It only upsets me. You don’t have a mother’s feelings, so you’re much better suited to it. You can get little Charles to do anything; one word from you and he obeys. That will be far better than leaving him with only Jemima. Oh, I shall certainly go! If I can, I’m sure I ought to, just as much as Charles. They’re extremely eager for me to meet Captain Wentworth, and I know you don’t mind being left alone. What a splendid idea, Anne. I’ll tell Charles and get ready immediately. You can send for us at once if anything goes wrong, you know, but I’m sure nothing will happen to frighten you. Of course I wouldn’t go unless I felt completely reassured about my dear child.”

A moment later she was knocking at her husband’s dressing-room door. Anne followed her upstairs and arrived in time to hear the entire conversation, which Mary began in a voice of great triumph:

“I’m coming with you, Charles, because I’m no more useful at home than you are. Even if I stayed shut up with the child forever, I couldn’t persuade him to do anything he didn’t want to do. Anne will stay. She’s agreed to remain at home and look after him. It was her own suggestion, so I’ll come with you, which will be much better. I haven’t had dinner at the other house since Tuesday.”

“That’s very kind of Anne,” her husband replied, “and I’d be very glad to have you come. But it does seem rather unfair that she should be left here by herself to nurse our sick child.”
